lcd-soundsystem-announces-12-show-holida.title: LCD Soundsystem Announces 12-Show Holiday Residency at Knockdown Center and Brooklyn Steel
lcd-soundsystem-announces-12-show-holida.dek: The band's annual New York residency includes its 100th residency show. Proceeds from that night will go to charity.
body: LCD Soundsystem has announced its annual holiday residency in New York, Resident Advisor reported. Twelve shows, split between Knockdown Center in Maspeth and Brooklyn Steel in East Williamsburg.
Eight of them are at Knockdown Center, on Nov. 19 to 22 and Dec. 10 to 13. Four are at Brooklyn Steel, from Nov. 30 to Dec. 3, according to RA. Openers and DJs have not been announced.

The Nov. 30 show at Brooklyn Steel will be the band's 100th residency show, RA reported. The tradition began in 2021. All ticket proceeds from that night will go to a charity that has not yet been named.

According to RA, the band has released no new material since the 2024 single "x-ray eyes." It toured the U.S. and Europe this year. It is scheduled to open for Harry Styles at a show in Rome, and it has three New Year's Eve dates in Aspen, Colorado.
Separately, guitarist Al Doyle, who also plays in Hot Chip, announced his debut solo album, Hollywood Saviour, RA reported. It is due Nov. 20 on DFA Records.

mass-and-cass-kimberly-webb-manslaughter.title: Two Plead Guilty in the 2023 Mass and Cass Stabbing Death of Kimberly Webb
mass-and-cass-kimberly-webb-manslaughter.dek: Michael Bellanti and Crystal Morgan pleaded guilty to manslaughter, ending first-degree murder cases in the killing of a 39-year-old mother of three.
body: Kimberly Webb was stabbed on a South End street at the edge of Mass and Cass three years ago. The two people charged with killing her have now pleaded guilty, according to Boston.com and Universal Hub. Both had been charged with murder. Both accepted manslaughter deals instead.

Michael Bellanti, 35, entered his plea in Suffolk Superior Court on Tuesday, Oct. 13, just as his first-degree murder trial was set to begin, Universal Hub reported. Judge James Budreau sentenced him to 10 to 15 years at the Souza Baranowski Correctional Center, with a little more than three years of credit for time already served.

Crystal Morgan, 41, was to begin her own first-degree murder trial the following day. On Wednesday morning, Oct. 14, she too pleaded guilty to manslaughter, and she was sentenced to six to eight years in state prison, Boston.com and Universal Hub reported. Universal Hub identified the judge in her case as Christopher Belezos.
## What Prosecutors Say Happened

The Suffolk County District Attorney's Office set out its account in court filings described by Boston.com and Universal Hub. It began as an argument among the three on Aug. 18, 2023, near Atkinson Street. Boston police officers broke up the fight and sent them off in opposite directions.

According to prosecutors, Webb walked toward Southampton and Topeka streets, while Bellanti and Morgan took a route that brought them back onto Topeka. Bellanti bent down and took an item from near his right sock, then approached Webb, with Morgan following, the DA's account said.

Prosecutors said Morgan held Webb's arm so she could not leave, while Bellanti backed her across the street and stabbed her in the chest, hand and arm. "Bellanti begins slashing and stabbing in the direction of Webb," the DA's office wrote, according to Universal Hub. The two then walked away toward Southampton Street.
Webb made her way back toward Atkinson Street and was taken to a hospital. She died nine days later, Boston.com reported.
## "A Smile That Lit Up a Room"
Webb was 39, a mother of three, and the caretaker for her mother, who uses a wheelchair, according to Boston.com. She had been struggling with the death of her sister.
Her best friend of more than three decades, whose name was not published, read a victim impact statement in court, Boston.com reported.
> "We had hope that she would get through this difficult time, get help, find sobriety, and rebuild her life." — Kimberly Webb's best friend, in a statement read in court, as reported by Boston.com
The friend described Webb as "absolutely hilarious," with "a smile that lit up a room," according to Boston.com.
## The Plea Agreements

Court filings show the murder charges were reduced to manslaughter under plea agreements, Boston.com reported. Defense attorneys Dmitry Lev, who represents Bellanti, and Daniel P. Fitzgerald, who represents Morgan, did not respond to Boston.com's requests for comment.

Bellanti will serve his sentence at Souza Baranowski, according to Universal Hub. The more than three years he spent in custody awaiting trial count toward it, so part of his minimum term is already behind him.

whitfield-street-dorchester-homicide-jos.title: Dorchester Man, 20, Charged With Murder a Day After Fatal Shooting on Whitfield Street
whitfield-street-dorchester-homicide-jos.dek: Joseph Bailey, 20, pleaded not guilty and was held without bail on a murder charge in a Sept. 30 shooting near 7 Whitfield Street in Dorchester.
body: The call came in at about 5:39 p.m. on Wednesday, Sept. 30, reporting a person shot near 7 Whitfield Street in Dorchester. Within roughly a day, Boston police had named a suspect and charged him with murder.

Joseph Bailey, 20, of Dorchester, was arraigned on Thursday, Oct. 1, in Dorchester District Court on a charge of murder, according to Boston.com, which cited court records. He pleaded not guilty and was ordered held without bail.
## The Shooting

Officers from District B-2, the Roxbury district, answered the radio call and found a man suffering from what appeared to be a gunshot wound, the Boston Police Department said in a news release. He was taken to a local hospital and later pronounced dead.
Police have not publicly identified him. As of Thursday evening, his name had not been released, Boston.com reported.

The shooting took place in Dorchester, but the first officers to arrive came from District B-2, which covers Roxbury and Mission Hill, according to the department's account. Police have released nothing about the man's age or where he lived.
## The Arrest

Detectives identified Bailey as a suspect after an investigation, the department said in its release. Police did not say where or how he was taken into custody, whether a weapon was recovered, or what may have led to the shooting. No motive has been made public.
The release included no comment from officials, and Boston.com reported that information about Bailey's attorney was not immediately available.
## What Comes Next

Bailey is due back in court on Oct. 22 for a probable cause hearing, according to Boston.com. In Massachusetts, murder cases that begin in district court typically move to superior court once a grand jury returns an indictment.
At a probable cause hearing, a judge decides whether there is enough evidence for the case to go forward. Prosecutors, though, frequently seek a grand jury indictment before that date arrives.

Police said the Homicide Unit is still investigating. Anyone with information is asked to call homicide detectives at 617-343-4470. Tips can be left anonymously with CrimeStoppers at 1-800-494-TIPS, or by texting the word TIP to CRIME (27463).
The city's Neighborhood Trauma Team offers free, confidential support around the clock to people affected by violence at 617-431-0125, the department said.
Bailey is presumed innocent unless and until he is proven guilty in court.

hopkinton-man-arraigned-on-attempted-mur.title: Hopkinton Man Pleads Not Guilty to Attempted Murder in Lake Maspenock Incident
hopkinton-man-arraigned-on-attempted-mur.dek: Prosecutors say a 70-year-old Hopkinton man held a 21-year-old under water at a local beach in June, after a dispute over a jet ski.
body: A 70-year-old Hopkinton man pleaded not guilty on Monday in Middlesex Superior Court to attempted murder and related charges arising from a June confrontation at Lake Maspenock, the Boston Globe reported.
Steven A. Dana is charged with attempted murder, strangulation or suffocation, and misdemeanor assault and battery, according to the Globe. A grand jury indicted him last month.

Police accounts described in court say the June 3 dispute began over a jet ski. Police allege that Dana confronted a group of young people because they did not live in the Hopkinton neighborhood that holds exclusive summer use of the beach's boat ramp. The argument escalated, authorities allege, and Dana slapped a 21-year-old Milford man, pushed him into the water and held him under for about 10 seconds before the man's friends pulled him away. The Globe reported that the incident was captured on video.

According to the Globe, police said Dana told them he was the victim, that two of the young men had forced him into the water, and that he repeated that account after learning a video existed. Dana's attorney declined to comment to the newspaper.

Dana was first arraigned in Framingham District Court and released on $7,500 bail. Judge Michael A. Sullivan approved moving that bail to the superior court case, the Globe reported, and Dana must stay away from the man and from the beach and may not possess weapons. His next pretrial hearing is set for Dec. 11. He is presumed innocent.

abington-mother-pleads-not-guilty-to-abu.title: Abington Woman Pleads Not Guilty to Charges of Abusing Her Infant
abington-mother-pleads-not-guilty-to-abu.dek: A 34-year-old Abington woman was arraigned in Plymouth Superior Court on charges that she seriously injured her 2-month-old daughter.
body: A 34-year-old Abington woman pleaded not guilty on Monday in Plymouth Superior Court in Brockton to charges that she physically abused her 2-month-old daughter, the Boston Globe reported.

She was indicted on Oct. 1 on a felony count of assault and battery on a child causing serious bodily injury, and on a misdemeanor count of reckless endangerment of a child, according to the Globe. She had been arrested in late July after an investigation, and had earlier pleaded not guilty in Brockton District Court.

The Plymouth District Attorney's office said the woman brought the infant to South Shore Hospital in Weymouth in early July. The baby had a dangerously low body temperature and bruising on her face, and was flown to the neonatal intensive care unit at Boston Children's Hospital, prosecutors said. A mandated reporter at the hospital alerted authorities. The DA's office said the infant had serious head injuries consistent with physical abuse.
In July, prosecutors said the injuries were severe enough that the child may face lasting disabilities.

At Monday's hearing, the woman was ordered to have no contact with an alleged co-defendant, and no contact with her daughter unless a Department of Children and Families supervisor or a health care professional requests it, the Globe reported. Her lawyer could not be reached for comment. She is due back in court on Nov. 17, and she is presumed innocent.

unlicensed-driver-accused-of-hitting-fou.title: Driver Cited After SUV Strikes Four Parked Cars and Overturns in Allston
unlicensed-driver-accused-of-hitting-fou.dek: Boston police said the driver, who was not injured, did not have a valid license and will be summonsed to Brighton District Court.
body: A driver was cited for operating without a valid license late Saturday after his SUV struck four parked cars and rolled onto its side on Park Vale Avenue in Allston, Boston police said, according to Boston.com.

Officers were called just before midnight to a report of a crash near 4 Park Vale Ave., police said, and found a black GMC Terrain lying on its driver's side in the middle of the street. The driver had gotten out of the vehicle and remained at the scene.

A preliminary investigation found that the GMC hit a parked Honda CR-V, then struck a second parked CR-V and pushed it into a parked Honda Accord. The SUV then rolled over and hit a Nissan Altima parked across the street, police said.

According to police, the driver reported no injuries and declined to be taken to a hospital. Officers determined that he did not have a valid license, and he was cited for unlicensed operation of a motor vehicle and for having no inspection sticker. The GMC was towed.
The driver, who was not named, will be summonsed to Brighton District Court, Boston.com reported. The department's Auto Investigations Unit is still investigating.

farwell-murder-trial-puts-focus-on-the-w.title: Globe Column Traces How Friends and Family Pushed for Answers in Farwell Case
farwell-murder-trial-puts-focus-on-the-w.dek: As the federal murder trial of former Stoughton police officer Matthew Farwell continues, a Globe columnist examines how the people close to the woman he is accused of killing kept her case alive.
body: A Boston Globe column published Oct. 17 looks at how the relatives and friends of a Canton woman pressed authorities to look again at her 2021 death, a death that is now at the center of the federal murder trial of former Stoughton police detective Matthew Farwell.

The woman, who was pregnant, was found dead in her Canton apartment in February 2021, according to the column by Yvonne Abraham. The state medical examiner and State Police first concluded that she had taken her own life. Her family later hired a forensic expert, who concluded she had been killed, the Globe reported, and relatives gave State Police a broken necklace found on the bedroom floor that an expert said suggested a struggle.

According to the column, a Stoughton police internal investigation authorized by Chief Donna McNamara found that Farwell and other officers had inappropriate relationships with the woman. Federal authorities arrested Farwell in August 2024.

Prosecutors allege that Farwell killed the woman to keep her from revealing abuse, and that he staged the scene. Farwell has pleaded not guilty, and his attorneys say she took her own life after he ended their relationship. He is presumed innocent.
The trial is underway in federal court in Boston. By the end of its first week, friends and relatives had testified about the plans she had for her future, according to the Globe.

texts-and-testimony-aired-at-farwell-mur.title: FBI Witnesses Detail Phone Evidence at Former Stoughton Officer's Trial
texts-and-testimony-aired-at-farwell-mur.dek: Federal investigators testified Friday about tens of thousands of messages and phone records in the trial of former Stoughton police detective Matthew Farwell.
body: On Friday, jurors in the federal trial of former Stoughton police detective Matthew Farwell heard FBI investigators describe the messages, search records and phone activity recovered in the case, according to Boston.com's live coverage from the Moakley federal courthouse in Boston.

Farwell is charged with killing a witness or victim and with killing a child in utero. Prosecutors allege that he killed a woman in early 2021 after learning she was pregnant with a child he believed was his, Boston.com reported. She was found dead in a Canton apartment. The defense contends that she died by suicide, which is the conclusion a state investigation first reached, before a federal investigation led to Farwell's indictment, according to the report.

FBI digital forensic examiner Christopher Beckstrom testified that investigators recovered about 240,000 communications from the woman's devices, roughly 24,000 of them with Farwell, Boston.com reported. On cross-examination, he agreed that she had sent far more of those messages than Farwell had. He also described searches on a phone linked to Farwell, and phone activity on the night of Feb. 1, 2021, the last day she was seen alive, according to the report.

Prosecutors say the woman had been an underage participant in a Stoughton police youth explorers program. Jurors heard messages describing sexual conduct when she was a minor, Boston.com reported. Kingston Police Chief Brian Holmes, a former Stoughton deputy chief, testified about an internal affairs investigation that found Farwell and other officers had engaged in inappropriate conduct with her.
FBI Special Agent Heidi Kelsch, who said the bureau interviewed about 130 people, was expected to resume her testimony on Monday. Farwell is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

former-healey-aide-lamar-cook-jailed-aga.title: Judge Revokes Bail for Former Healey Aide LaMar Cook After Federal Fraud Charges
former-healey-aide-lamar-cook-jailed-aga.dek: A Hampden County judge sent Cook back to jail for 90 days, one day after federal prosecutors charged him with SNAP fraud and wire fraud.
body: LaMar D. Cook, a former aide to Gov. Maura Healey who already faces gun and drug trafficking charges, was ordered back to jail on Thursday after federal prosecutors charged him with fraud, the Boston Globe reported.

Hampden County Judge David Hodge granted a motion by state prosecutors to revoke Cook's bail in his state case, and ordered him held for 90 days, according to the Globe. Prosecutors argued that there was probable cause he had violated federal law, and that he was unlikely to follow the conditions of his release.

On Wednesday, the U.S. Attorney's Office in Massachusetts charged Cook, 46, of Springfield, with SNAP fraud and wire fraud. Federal prosecutors allege that he received nearly $550 a month in food assistance by falsely claiming he had no income and less than $100 in the bank, while his balance was about $13,000 in January, the Globe reported. He was released after a federal hearing on Wednesday.

Cook was arrested in October 2025 after police allegedly seized about 17 pounds of cocaine that was to be delivered to the Springfield state building where he worked for Healey. He was released on $25,000 bail in March.

His lawyer, Kedar Ismail, said he respects the judge's decision and looks forward to clearing Cook's name, and argued in court that the motion was political. U.S. Attorney Leah B. Foley criticized the state's oversight. Healey, who appointed Cook in 2023, said it was good that he had been charged, according to the Globe. Cook is presumed innocent.

jury-orders-boston-water-and-sewer-commi.title: Jury Orders Boston Water and Sewer Commission to Pay $1 Million for Retaliation
jury-orders-boston-water-and-sewer-commi.dek: A Suffolk County jury rejected a former manager's discrimination claims but found the commission retaliated against him after he sued. The commission plans to appeal.
body: A Suffolk County jury on Thursday ordered the Boston Water and Sewer Commission to pay $1 million to a former employee, finding that the agency retaliated against him after he sued over alleged racial discrimination, the Boston Globe reported.

The jury rejected the discrimination claims themselves, which were brought by Terrance Williams, a Black Dorchester resident who joined the commission in 1988 and became manager of operations in 2017, according to the Globe. The award includes $400,000 in punitive damages, his attorney said.

Williams sued in 2022, alleging that the commission underpaid Black employees, himself among them, and passed them over in favor of less experienced white colleagues. He said that after he filed suit he was reprimanded over a parking spot, had his performance reviews altered and was denied promotion interviews. He was fired in May 2025.

His attorney, Nick Carter, told the Globe that the commission fired Williams for standing up for Black workers, and urged city and state leaders to scrutinize the agency. Commission attorney Brian T. Kelly said the agency was pleased the jury rejected the discrimination claims and will appeal the retaliation finding. Kelly said Williams was fired for working a second job with the sheriff's department while on the clock.
The commission serves more than a million people daily and employs about 450 people, according to the Globe.

friend-testifies-at-farwell-trial.title: Friend and Stoughton Police Chief Testify at Farwell Federal Trial
friend-testifies-at-farwell-trial.dek: A friend of the woman told jurors she urged Canton police to look at former detective Matthew Farwell after the death, the Boston Globe reported.
body: A close friend of the woman whose 2021 death is at the center of former Stoughton police detective Matthew Farwell's federal trial testified on Thursday that, after the death, she went to Canton police and encouraged them to investigate Farwell, the Boston Globe reported.

Farwell, 40, is on trial in U.S. District Court in Boston before Chief Judge Denise J. Casper. Prosecutors allege that he killed the 23-year-old woman, who was pregnant, in February 2021, to keep her from reporting crimes that included an illegal sexual relationship that began when she was 15, according to the Globe. The defense argues that she died by suicide. The state medical examiner first ruled the death a suicide and later changed the finding to undetermined, the newspaper reported.

The friend testified that the woman wanted to have Farwell's child, and that she had told her Farwell said the child was not his, according to the Globe. She said she spoke with the woman by phone days before her death and noticed nothing unusual.

Stoughton Police Chief Donna McNamara, who is on leave, testified that she did not know about a January 2021 call to the department concerning the woman until an FBI agent told her in 2024, the Globe reported. A digital forensic analyst testified about extracting data from the woman's devices, and the defense signaled that it will argue a manual review of her laptop altered data, according to the report. Kingston Police Chief Brian Holmes, a former Stoughton deputy chief, began his testimony about the department's internal investigation.
Farwell has been held without bail since his arrest in August 2024, and he faces life in prison if convicted, the Globe reported. He is presumed innocent.

key-witnesses-testify-in-farwell-trial.title: Forensic Analyst and Police Officials Take the Stand in Farwell Trial
key-witnesses-testify-in-farwell-trial.dek: Thursday's testimony in the federal trial of former Stoughton detective Matthew Farwell covered device searches, a deleted station call recording and an internal investigation.
body: On Thursday, the third day of testimony in the federal trial of former Stoughton police detective Matthew Farwell, jurors heard from a state police digital forensics examiner, two current and former Stoughton police leaders, a Stoughton officer and a friend of the woman who died, Boston.com reported.

Farwell is charged with killing a witness or victim and with killing a child in utero. The woman was found dead in her Canton apartment in February 2021. A state investigation first ruled the death a suicide, but an FBI investigation later led to Farwell's indictment, according to the report. Farwell maintains that she died by suicide after he ended their relationship. Prosecutors allege that he killed her to keep her from speaking about the relationship and about alleged misconduct.

Trooper Nicholas Guarino testified about accessing the woman's phone and laptop, and said a search of Farwell's iPhone in February 2021 turned up nothing before the phone was returned, according to Boston.com. On cross-examination, he said some extraction data had been deleted as redundant, and that he could not find a report on a failed hard drive.

Former Stoughton Deputy Chief Brian Holmes, now Kingston's police chief, testified that a January 2021 call to the station from the woman's friend was recorded but later deleted automatically, the report said. Stoughton Chief Donna McNamara, who is on paid leave, reviewed attendance logs and the station call log. Prosecutors say Farwell grew worried after that call.

The friend testified that the woman seemed unhappy but not suicidal, and that their last call was around 8:30 p.m. on Feb. 1, 2021, according to Boston.com. Holmes was scheduled to return to the stand Friday. Farwell is presumed innocent.

boston-schools-employee-charged-with-rap.title: Boston Schools Employee Pleads Not Guilty to Rape Charge in Oak Bluffs Case
boston-schools-employee-charged-with-rap.dek: Prosecutors allege a Boston Public Schools security employee assaulted a woman at the State Police barracks on Martha's Vineyard this summer.
body: A Boston Public Schools security employee pleaded not guilty on Tuesday in Edgartown District Court to raping a woman this summer at the State Police barracks in Oak Bluffs, on Martha's Vineyard, according to Boston.com.

Edward Joseph Brown, 27, of Boston, was arrested on Oct. 9 at Boston Latin Academy by Oak Bluffs and Boston police, Boston.com reported. Prosecutors said police found suspected cocaine in his wallet when he was arrested.

According to prosecutors, the woman told police that she met a man at a bar who bought her a drink, and that she later woke up with him in an unfamiliar place. Prosecutors said cellphone data tracked a rideshare trip to the barracks. A state trooper told investigators that Brown had been visiting him on the island that week, according to Boston.com.

Brown is being held at the Dukes County jail on $10,000 cash bail and is due back in court on Dec. 3. His lawyer, Anthony Ellison, said Brown maintains his innocence and looks forward to trial. He is presumed innocent.

Boston Public Schools placed Brown on administrative leave and said the charges do not involve students. Oak Bluffs police said the arrest followed an independent investigation conducted with the Cape and Islands District Attorney's Office, and that the case remains under investigation. State Police have opened an internal probe.

boston-man-sentenced-in-2023-fatal-stabb.title: Two Sentenced to Prison for 2023 Fatal Stabbing Near Mass. and Cass
boston-man-sentenced-in-2023-fatal-stabb.dek: Both defendants pleaded guilty to manslaughter in the death of a 39-year-old woman on Topeka Street, the Suffolk District Attorney's office said.
body: Two Boston residents have been sentenced to state prison after pleading guilty to manslaughter in the 2023 fatal stabbing of a woman near Massachusetts Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard, the Boston Globe reported, citing the Suffolk District Attorney's office.

Michael Bellanti, 35, was sentenced on Tuesday to 10 to 15 years in prison, according to the Globe. Crystal Morgan, 41, was scheduled to begin jury selection on Wednesday in Suffolk Superior Court. Instead she pleaded guilty, and she was sentenced to six to eight years, the DA's office said.

According to prosecutors, the attack took place on the evening of Aug. 18, 2023, on Topeka Street, after Boston police broke up a fight on nearby Atkinson Street. Prosecutors said Bellanti approached the 39-year-old woman and stabbed her while Morgan held her arm and kept her from leaving. The woman was taken to a hospital, where she died.
At her arraignment in 2023, Morgan had pleaded not guilty to second-degree murder, according to court records cited by the Globe.

In court, a statement from a friend of the woman was read, describing her as more than the circumstances of her death. District Attorney Kevin R. Hayden said the friend's words carried an important message about her life.

state-trooper-describes-first-farwell-in.title: State Trooper Describes First Interview With Matthew Farwell at Trial
state-trooper-describes-first-farwell-in.dek: A state police investigator testified that the 2021 parking-lot interview with the former Stoughton detective was not recorded, and that Farwell lied during it.
body: A Massachusetts State Police trooper testified on Wednesday that investigators interviewed former Stoughton police detective Matthew Farwell in a school parking lot days after a woman's death in 2021, and that Farwell lied during that conversation, Boston.com reported from Farwell's federal trial in Boston.

Farwell is charged with killing a witness or victim and with killing a child in utero. The woman was found dead in her Canton apartment in February 2021. A state investigation first ruled the death a suicide, before an FBI investigation led to his indictment, according to the report.

Trooper Matthew Dunne, assigned to the Norfolk County District Attorney's office, testified that investigators identified Farwell on surveillance footage on Feb. 6, 2021, and chose to interview him quickly and away from his home and workplace, Boston.com reported. The interview was not recorded, and no notes were taken. Dunne described both as tactical decisions made by a supervisor. He said Farwell told investigators he visited the woman on Feb. 1, 2021, to end their relationship, and that Farwell lied about when the relationship began and how often it was sexual.

Under cross-examination by defense attorney Kimberly Stevens, Dunne confirmed that DNA testing excluded Farwell as the father of the woman's unborn child, according to the report. The defense also pointed to the absence of signs of a struggle, and to the woman's mental health history. Dunne acknowledged that some items at the scene were not collected and that neighbors were not interviewed.
A state toxicologist and Stoughton officer Robert Kuhn also testified, Boston.com reported. Testimony was set to resume on Thursday. Farwell is presumed innocent.

second-guilty-plea-in-2023-stabbing-of-w.title: Second Defendant Pleads Guilty to Manslaughter in 2023 Mass and Cass Killing
second-guilty-plea-in-2023-stabbing-of-w.dek: A 41-year-old Boston woman was sentenced to six to eight years in prison for her role in the fatal stabbing of a 39-year-old woman on Topeka Street, prosecutors said.
body: A second defendant has pleaded guilty to manslaughter in the 2023 stabbing death of a 39-year-old woman near the area known as Mass and Cass, the Suffolk County District Attorney's Office said.

Crystal Morgan, 41, of Boston, entered her plea in Suffolk Superior Court and was sentenced by Judge Christopher Belezos to six to eight years in state prison, according to a release from the office. Her co-defendant, Michael Bellanti, 35, of Boston, had pleaded guilty to manslaughter on Tuesday and was sentenced by Judge James Budreau to 10 to 15 years in state prison, prosecutors said.

According to prosecutors, an altercation involving the woman, Morgan and Bellanti began on the evening of Aug. 18, 2023, on Atkinson Street. Police broke up the dispute and separated the three, the release said.

Prosecutors said surveillance evidence showed that Bellanti and Morgan later followed the woman onto Topeka Street, where Bellanti attacked her while Morgan held her. Both then left the area, according to the release. The woman died of her injuries on Aug. 27, 2023, nine days later, prosecutors said.

District Attorney Kevin Hayden said the court received a statement from the woman's best friend that described her as a mother of three, a godmother and a close friend, according to the release. Hayden thanked the friend for helping the court see the woman's life beyond the circumstances of her death.

coworker-testifies-suicide-reports-did-n.title: Former School Colleague Testifies as Testimony Begins in Farwell Trial
coworker-testifies-suicide-reports-did-n.dek: A former assistant principal told jurors that reports the woman died by suicide did not fit the person she knew, the Boston Globe reported.
body: Testimony began on Tuesday in the federal trial of former Stoughton police detective Matthew Farwell. The first witness, a former school administrator, told jurors that reports the woman at the center of the case had died by suicide did not make sense to her, the Boston Globe reported.

Prosecutors allege that Farwell groomed the woman when she was a child in the Stoughton police Explorers program, began an illegal sexual relationship with her when she was 15 and he was 27, and killed her in 2021 to cover up those crimes, according to the Globe. The defense argues that she was upset because Farwell was ending their relationship, and that she died by suicide. Farwell has pleaded not guilty.

The former assistant principal at the Sharon elementary school where the woman worked as a teacher's aide testified that the woman was excited about her pregnancy, the Globe reported. She said she requested a wellness check when the woman missed work. On cross-examination, the defense questioned the woman's work record, and the witness's membership in an online group seeking justice in the case.

Stoughton Det. Heather Cheever, who mentored the woman in the Explorers program, testified that the woman never expressed suicidal thoughts to her, according to the Globe. A property manager testified that she and a coworker reviewed security footage showing a masked, hooded figure who was later identified as Farwell. A Canton officer described finding the woman during a well-being check.

Chief U.S. District Judge Denise J. Casper is presiding over the trial, which is expected to last about five weeks, the Globe reported. Farwell has been held without bail since his arrest in 2024, and he is presumed innocent.

victim-identified-in-whitfield-street-ho.title: Police Identify Man Killed in Whitfield Street Shooting in Dorchester
victim-identified-in-whitfield-street-ho.dek: Boston police said a 21-year-old Dorchester man died after a Sept. 30 shooting. A 20-year-old has been arraigned on a murder charge.
body: Boston police have identified the man fatally shot on Whitfield Street in Dorchester last month as a 21-year-old Dorchester resident, according to a department update.

Officers from District B-2 responded at about 5:39 p.m. on Wednesday, Sept. 30, to a report of a person shot in the area of 7 Whitfield St., police said. They found the man with an apparent gunshot wound and took him to a local hospital, where he was later pronounced dead.
Detectives identified Joseph Bailey, 20, of Dorchester, as a suspect, according to the department. Bailey has been arraigned in Dorchester District Court on a murder charge. He is presumed innocent.

The department's Homicide Unit is still reviewing the case, police said. Anyone with information is asked to call homicide detectives at 617-343-4470. Anonymous tips can be made through CrimeStoppers at 1-800-494-TIPS, or by texting TIP to 27463.
The Boston Neighborhood Trauma Team offers free, confidential support around the clock at 617-431-0125, according to the department.

farwell-murder-trial-opens.title: Opening Statements Delivered in Federal Trial of Former Stoughton Detective
farwell-murder-trial-opens.dek: Prosecutors told jurors Matthew Farwell killed a woman to cover up years of abuse. The defense said her 2021 death was a suicide, the Boston Globe reported.
body: The federal trial of former Stoughton police detective Matthew Farwell opened on Friday at the Moakley U.S. Courthouse in Boston, with statements from prosecutors and from the defense, the Boston Globe reported.

Farwell is charged with killing a woman to stop her from reporting federal crimes, and with causing the death of her fetus, according to the Globe. He has pleaded not guilty and has been held without bail since his arrest in 2024. Chief U.S. District Judge Denise J. Casper is presiding. A jury of 10 men and six women was seated for a trial expected to last about five weeks.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Torey B. Cummings told jurors that Farwell killed the woman in February 2021 at her Canton apartment and staged the scene to look like a suicide, the Globe reported. She argued that he had sexually abused the woman for years, beginning when she was a teenager, and that state police investigators had told the medical examiner the death was a suicide. DNA evidence has ruled out Farwell as the father of the baby, according to the report.

Defense attorney Kimberly C. Stevens acknowledged that Farwell made serious mistakes, but said he did not kill the woman, according to the Globe. She argued that Farwell had ended the relationship and denied paternity, and that the woman, facing financial and emotional stress, took her own life. Stevens also challenged the forensic evidence.

Testimony was set to begin on Tuesday, after the Monday holiday. Prosecutors planned to call six witnesses, among them a Stoughton detective, a school administrator and officers who responded to the apartment, the Globe reported. Farwell is presumed innocent.

jury-pool-trimmed-for-farwell-trial.title: Lawyers Recommend Excusing a Quarter of Jury Pool in Farwell Trial
jury-pool-trimmed-for-farwell-trial.dek: Prosecutors and the defense jointly proposed dismissing 102 of 411 prospective jurors in the federal murder trial of former Stoughton detective Matthew Farwell, the Boston Globe reported.
body: On Wednesday, prosecutors and defense lawyers in the federal murder trial of former Stoughton police detective Matthew Farwell jointly recommended that 102 of the 411 prospective jurors be excused, about a quarter of the initial pool, the Boston Globe reported.

Chief U.S. District Judge Denise J. Casper took the recommendation under advisement at a brief hearing, according to the Globe. Both sides were also reviewing questionnaires from 44 more potential jurors. Jury selection began on Tuesday, when prospective jurors filled out questionnaires that the court is keeping confidential, the newspaper reported.

Jurors who advance were due back on Thursday for individual questioning, and Casper planned to seat 16 jurors, four of them alternates, according to the Globe. Lawyers were told to be ready for opening statements on Friday. Testimony is expected to last about five weeks, with more than 100 possible witnesses.

Farwell, 40, is charged in the death of a 23-year-old woman who was found in her Canton apartment on Feb. 4, 2021, and he has pleaded not guilty, the Globe reported. Prosecutors allege that he killed her to conceal years of crimes, including an illegal sexual relationship that began when she was 15. The defense says she died by suicide.

An initial investigation by Norfolk District Attorney Michael W. Morrissey's office concluded the death was a suicide. The FBI arrested Farwell in 2024, according to the Globe. Farwell twice sought, without success, to move the trial out of Massachusetts, arguing that news coverage had affected the jury pool. He is presumed innocent.

acton-teen-arraigned-in-killing-of-his-m.title: Acton Teen Pleads Not Guilty to Murder in Deaths of Mother and Brother
acton-teen-arraigned-in-killing-of-his-m.dek: A 17-year-old from Acton pleaded not guilty Tuesday in Middlesex Superior Court to murder charges in the August deaths of his mother and younger brother.
body: A 17-year-old from Acton pleaded not guilty on Tuesday in Middlesex County Superior Court to charges that he killed his mother and his 14-year-old brother, Boston.com reported.

He is charged with murder and assault in the deaths of his mother, who was 45, and his brother, and with one count of motor vehicle theft, according to the report. Judge Michael A. Sullivan ordered him held without bail under an agreement between prosecutors and the defense, Boston.com reported. The next step is a scheduling conference on Oct. 27.

Prosecutors allege that the deaths occurred on Aug. 11 at the family's home in Acton. According to the Middlesex District Attorney's office, the father asked police to conduct a wellness check after a tutor arrived at the house that evening and got no answer. Officers found both victims inside the home, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors allege that the teen left in his mother's car after the killings. Police found him and the vehicle in a Wayland parking lot at about 3:30 a.m. the next day and took him into custody without incident, according to the report.

He was first arraigned in Concord District Court on Aug. 13, and a grand jury indicted him on Oct. 1, Boston.com reported. His attorney did not respond to requests for comment. The charges are allegations, and he is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

massachusetts-man-pleads-guilty-in-schem.title: Hadley Man Pleads Guilty to Importing and Selling Russian Plutonium
massachusetts-man-pleads-guilty-in-schem.dek: A 44-year-old Hadley man pleaded guilty in federal court to five counts, including importing nuclear material from Russia and mailing hazardous materials to customers.
body: A Hadley man has pleaded guilty in federal court to illegally importing plutonium from Russia and selling it to customers in the United States and abroad, according to Boston.com, which cited the U.S. Attorney's Office in Massachusetts.

Jacob Miller, 44, pleaded guilty to five counts, the report said: being a felon in possession of ammunition, being a felon in possession of explosive materials, importing nuclear material without lawful authority, mailing hazardous materials, and possession of child pornography. In 2004 he had been sentenced to six months in prison and 10 years of probation for possessing child pornography and an explosive device.

According to prosecutors, Miller ran a business from his home that sold samples of chemical elements, both directly and through an online retailer. Prosecutors said he mailed plutonium to about 67 customers between December 2020 and March 2025. He also sold thallium, another hazardous substance that cannot legally be mailed, to about 71 customers between 2017 and April 2025.

Authorities searched his home in April 2025 and reported finding explosive powder, ammunition and six rifles, all of which he was barred from having because of his prior convictions, Boston.com reported. Prosecutors said his laptop and phone contained child sexual abuse material. He was arrested on April 9, 2025.

The nuclear import charge carries up to 20 years in prison, according to the report, and because of his prior conviction, the child pornography charge carries a mandatory minimum of 10 years. U.S. District Judge Mark G. Mastroianni set sentencing for Jan. 21, 2027.

inquest-finds-fatal-cambridge-police-sho.title: Inquest Finds Fatal Cambridge Police Shooting Justified; Bodycam Footage Released
inquest-finds-fatal-cambridge-police-sho.dek: A judge ruled that officers acted reasonably when they shot a 64-year-old Watertown man in Central Square in August. The district attorney will not file charges.
body: A judicial inquest has found that Cambridge police officers were justified when they fatally shot a 64-year-old Watertown man in Central Square in August, Boston.com reported. The Cambridge Police Department has released body-worn camera footage of the encounter.

The shooting took place on Temple Street shortly before 8 p.m. on Aug. 21, according to the report. A security guard at 675 Massachusetts Ave. had called 911 about people loitering in a nearby private parking lot, and Officer Donald Conrad approached a parked car with the man in the driver's seat.

According to the inquest findings as described by Boston.com, the man reached under the seat and pulled out a gun as Conrad ordered him out of the car. He ignored three commands to drop it, and pointed it at Officer David Kerns, who struggled with him. Conrad fired several shots and Officer James Nestor fired once, the judge found. The man died at the scene. The judge found that less than a minute passed between the start of the encounter and the shooting, and that the gun was loaded.

In a nine-page report, Judge Holly Broadbent concluded that the officers' use of force was objectively reasonable, and that any reasonable officer would have believed officers and civilians faced imminent danger, according to the report.

Middlesex District Attorney Marian Ryan's office accepted the findings and will not pursue criminal charges, Boston.com reported. Cambridge police said the footage provides context for a rapidly evolving situation. The department said no officers were seriously hurt, and offered condolences to the man's family.

man-20-charged-with-murder-in-fatal-dorc.title: Dorchester Man, 20, Charged With Murder in Whitfield Street Shooting
man-20-charged-with-murder-in-fatal-dorc.dek: A 20-year-old Dorchester man pleaded not guilty and was held without bail in the fatal shooting of a man near 7 Whitfield St., the Boston Globe reported.
body: A 20-year-old Dorchester man has been charged with murder in a fatal shooting on Whitfield Street in Dorchester, the Boston Globe reported.

Joseph Bailey was arraigned on Thursday, Oct. 1, in the Dorchester Division of Boston Municipal Court, where he was ordered held without bail, according to the Globe. Online court records show that he pleaded not guilty, the newspaper reported. No attorney was listed for him in those records.

Police said the shooting happened shortly before 5:40 p.m. on Wednesday, Sept. 30, near 7 Whitfield St., according to the Globe. A man was killed. Authorities had not released his name or his age, the newspaper reported.
Police said Bailey was arrested after an investigation, and a spokesperson for the Suffolk District Attorney's Office confirmed the murder charge, the Globe reported.
Bailey is scheduled to return to court on Oct. 22. The charge is an allegation, and he is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

man-20-facing-murder-charges-in-dorchest.title: Man, 20, Pleads Not Guilty to Murder in Fatal Dorchester Shooting
man-20-facing-murder-charges-in-dorchest.dek: A 20-year-old Dorchester man was ordered held without bail Thursday in the Sept. 30 shooting death near 7 Whitfield St., Boston.com reported.
body: A 20-year-old Dorchester man pleaded not guilty on Thursday to a murder charge in a fatal shooting near 7 Whitfield St. in Dorchester, and he was ordered held without bail, Boston.com reported.

Joseph Bailey was arraigned on Oct. 1 in Dorchester. He is due back in court on Oct. 22 for a probable cause hearing, according to the report. Information about his attorney was not immediately available.

The shooting happened shortly before 5:40 p.m. on Wednesday, Sept. 30, according to Boston.com. Officers found a person with a gunshot wound near the Whitfield Street address, and the man was taken to a local hospital, where he later died, the report said. As of Thursday evening, authorities had not publicly identified him.

In a press release, the Boston Police Department said authorities identified Bailey as the suspect after an investigation, Boston.com reported. He was arrested and charged with murder following that investigation, according to the report.
Bailey remains in custody. No court proceedings beyond the Oct. 22 hearing were reported. The murder charge is an allegation, and Bailey is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

fresh-meadows-man-indicted-on-hate-crime.title: Fresh Meadows Man Indicted on Hate Crime Charges Over Bagel Shop Vandalism
fresh-meadows-man-indicted-on-hate-crime.dek: Prosecutors say a 22-year-old twice damaged planters outside a kosher bagel shop on Union Turnpike that displayed Israeli flags.
body: A 22-year-old Fresh Meadows man has been indicted on two counts of third-degree criminal mischief as a hate crime, accused of vandalizing a kosher bagel shop on Union Turnpike that displayed Israeli flags, QNS reported, citing the Queens District Attorney's Office.

Dawood Faisal was arraigned on Oct. 19 in Queens Supreme Court, according to QNS. Prosecutors allege that at about 6:18 p.m. on May 15, he knocked over nine metal plant stands outside Bagels & Co. at 188-02 Union Turnpike and threw the debris at the shop.
Prosecutors further allege that at about 1 a.m. on May 23, he pushed and kicked over 11 plant stands, then pulled plants by hand from a large clay pot, QNS reported.

Queens District Attorney Melinda Katz said he allegedly targeted the business because it is Jewish-owned and displayed Israeli flags, and called bias crimes an affront to the community. The charge is not bail-eligible. Justice Michael Hartofilis ordered him to return to court on Nov. 12. If convicted, he faces up to seven years in prison, according to QNS.

Faisal is separately charged with manslaughter and assault in a May 25 crash near Cunningham Park that killed a 71-year-old woman, and he is being held without bail in that case, QNS reported. He is presumed innocent in both cases.

contractor-pleads-guilty-after-10-drywal.title: Contractor Pleads Guilty After 10 Drywall Workers Go Unpaid on UWS Job
contractor-pleads-guilty-after-10-drywal.dek: KEP Construction LLC pleaded guilty to grand larceny and scheme to defraud over $67,275 in wages withheld from immigrant workers.
body: KEP Construction LLC has pleaded guilty to grand larceny and scheme to defraud, after prosecutors said it withheld $67,275 in pay from 10 drywall workers, Hoodline reported.

Prosecutors said the company received more than $1.3 million from a general contractor for work on several buildings, among them a 23-story high-rise at 270 West 96th Street on the Upper West Side, according to Hoodline. The workers were owed for work done between September 2023 and February 2024, in individual amounts ranging from $2,600 to $11,000, according to court records cited from Upper West Side Patch.

Some workers received checks that bounced, and some received no payment at all, Hoodline reported. All 10 were immigrants and non-native English speakers, according to court records. The investigation began after workers repeatedly texted the company's owner, pleading for their wages.
The owner, Kendis Paul, was indicted in January 2025 and has pleaded not guilty, according to Hoodline. He is presumed innocent. The report did not include sentencing information for the company.

Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg announced that nearly $70,000 in wages had been returned to the workers, Hoodline reported. The Workers' Justice Project helped the workers file claims with the state Department of Labor, according to Documented NY.

officer-struck-by-suv-on-loud-music-call.title: Officer Struck by SUV on Loud-Music Call in Hunts Point; Driver at Large
officer-struck-by-suv-on-loud-music-call.dek: An NYPD officer suffered a leg injury when a driver in a white Honda SUV struck him and fled, police said.
body: An NYPD officer answering a loud-music complaint in Hunts Point was struck by a white Honda SUV, and the driver fled, Hoodline reported, citing police.

It happened at about 7:20 p.m. on Saturday at Garrison Avenue and Whittier Street, in the 41st Precinct, according to Hoodline. Several officers had responded to the complaint and found a large crowd. A person from the crowd drove off in the SUV and struck the officer, police said, as cited by News12 New York.
The officer suffered a leg injury and was taken by paramedics to Lincoln Hospital, according to Hoodline. Police said he is expected to recover. His name and age were not released.
Police said the driver sped away after the crash. No description of the driver has been released, Hoodline reported.
As of Saturday night, no arrests had been announced, and the investigation was ongoing, according to Hoodline. Anyone with information can contact NYPD Crime Stoppers at 1-800-577-TIPS.

indicted-deed-theft-suspect-now-says-her.title: Indicted Deed-Theft Suspect Now Says Her Own Home Was Stolen
indicted-deed-theft-suspect-now-says-her.dek: A Manhattan woman charged in the alleged theft of a dying Kew Gardens Hills widow's home has sued her co-defendant, claiming he took her Flushing house.
body: A 69-year-old Manhattan woman indicted in the alleged deed theft of a Kew Gardens Hills home now claims that her co-defendant also stole her own property in Flushing, Hoodline reported.

Deepa V. Roy and Victor Quimis were indicted in August 2025, accused of forging the signature of an 88-year-old homeowner in hospice care in 2024 in order to transfer her house to themselves, according to Hoodline. The woman died in June 2025. Both have pleaded not guilty and are due back in court on Nov. 4. Both are presumed innocent.

In a lawsuit filed Sept. 16 in Queens Supreme Court, first reported by the New York Post, Roy alleges that Quimis took her Flushing house after her husband died in 2023, Hoodline reported. She says she had asked him to help remove squatters, and that he instead created deeds making himself the owner. She is seeking at least $1 million.

Roy's criminal attorney, Jeremy Saland, said she disputes the allegations and may herself have been a victim of Quimis, according to Hoodline. The late homeowner's son told the Post he believes Roy is trying to deflect blame. Quimis and his lawyers did not respond to requests for comment.

The Times reported that the case was the first indictment under New York's law treating deed theft as grand larceny. Complaints to the attorney general's office rose from 149 in 2023 to 517 in 2025, according to CBS News New York.

maduro-calls-new-torture-allegations-fal.title: Maduro Calls New Torture Allegations False in Manhattan Federal Court
maduro-calls-new-torture-allegations-fal.dek: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro twice declined to enter a plea to a rewritten indictment, and a judge entered a not guilty plea on his behalf.
body: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro told a Manhattan federal court on Thursday that newly unsealed torture allegations against him and his wife, Cilia Flores, are false, the Associated Press reported in a story published by NY1.

The rewritten indictment expands the earlier drug trafficking charges and accuses the couple of leading a state-sponsored campaign of repression that tortured scores of people, three Americans among them, according to the AP. Prosecutors allege that Maduro oversaw the system and personally recommended methods, and that Flores, a former attorney general, helped develop it and ordered the torture of specific people. The charges cover alleged conduct beginning in 2013.

Speaking through an interpreter, Maduro twice declined to enter a plea, calling the charges false accusations and false testimony. U.S. District Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein entered a not guilty plea for him. Flores told the court she is innocent. Defense attorney Barry Pollack said Maduro denies the charges and looks forward to his day in court. Both are presumed innocent.

U.S. military forces took the couple from their home in Caracas in a nighttime raid in January, the AP reported. Earlier this year, they pleaded not guilty to charges of conspiring to send cocaine into the United States. Their lawyers argue that case should be dismissed on grounds of head-of-state immunity.
The judge set trial for June 14, 2027. Before then, the couple is scheduled to return to court for a pretrial hearing on Dec. 17.

two-men-plead-not-guilty-in-stabbing-and.title: Two Men Plead Not Guilty in Stabbing and Robbery of Off-Duty NYPD Detective
two-men-plead-not-guilty-in-stabbing-and.dek: Sneider Mejia and Dangelo Caraballo face charges including attempted murder in the Oct. 2 attack on an off-duty detective in Norwood, the Bronx.
body: Two men accused of stabbing and robbing an off-duty NYPD detective in the Bronx pleaded not guilty on Wednesday, News 12 reported.

Sneider Mejia, 24, and Dangelo Caraballo, 25, face charges that include attempted murder, robbery and assault on a police officer, according to News 12. Prosecutors asked that both men remain in custody, arguing that they are flight risks, and the judge ordered them held pending bail applications. Defense lawyers noted that family members were in court. Both men are presumed innocent.

Police said the attack happened at about 1:44 p.m. on Oct. 2, near Rochambeau Avenue and East 208th Street in Norwood. According to police, two men on a motorized bike approached the 33-year-old detective, who was off duty and on vacation, stabbed him several times, took a chain from his neck and rode away. He was treated at Jacobi Hospital and has since been released.

Police said the two suspects were later found hiding in a basement in Lynn, Massachusetts, and were brought back to New York. The Department of Homeland Security said both men are Dominican nationals living in the U.S. without legal status, and that both have prior arrests in New York, News 12 reported.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, the detective said that during the attack he identified himself as a police officer in English and in Spanish, and that he chased the men for about five blocks before a bystander called 911. He said he is still recovering from his injuries.

far-rockaway-teen-charged-in-killing-of-.title: Far Rockaway Teen Charged With Murder in Killing of 14-Year-Old in Arverne
far-rockaway-teen-charged-in-killing-of-.dek: A 17-year-old was arraigned on a second-degree murder charge, accused of fatally shooting a 14-year-old boy at the Ocean Bay Apartments on Sept. 21, QNS reported.
body: A 17-year-old from Far Rockaway was arraigned on Wednesday, Oct. 14, in Queens Supreme Court on a charge of second-degree murder and two counts of second-degree criminal possession of a weapon, in the fatal shooting of a 14-year-old boy in Arverne, according to QNS.

According to the criminal complaint cited by the outlet, the boy and three others arrived on push scooters at the courtyard of the Ocean Bay Apartments at about 3:33 p.m. on Sept. 21. Prosecutors allege that the defendant approached the boy beside a residential building at 51-24 Beach Channel Drive and fired two shots.

One bullet struck the boy in the lower back, according to the complaint. EMS took him to Cohen Children's Medical Center in Glen Oaks, where he underwent emergency surgery and was later pronounced dead, QNS reported.

Prosecutors allege that the teen then took the boy's scooter, fled east on Norton Avenue and changed his clothes in a public bathroom. Police later recovered the clothing from a trash bin in that bathroom, according to the report.
Queens District Attorney Melinda Katz called the killing targeted and execution-style, the outlet reported.

Justice Seth Steed ordered the defendant held without bail and set a return date of Oct. 19, according to QNS. If convicted, he faces up to 25 years to life in prison. The charges are accusations, and the defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

sunset-park-federal-jail-officer-indicte.title: Federal Jail Officer in Sunset Park Indicted in Contraband Bribery Case
sunset-park-federal-jail-officer-indicte.dek: A correctional officer at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn is accused of taking cash from inmates' associates to smuggle contraband into the jail, federal prosecutors said.
body: A federal correctional officer at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn has been indicted on charges that she took bribes to smuggle contraband into the Sunset Park jail, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of New York.

Melissa Brooks, 37, of Brooklyn, who has worked for the Federal Bureau of Prisons since July 2024, is charged with taking bribes as a public official and with conspiracy to do so, prosecutors said. She was arrested on the morning of Oct. 14, and was scheduled to be arraigned that afternoon before U.S. Magistrate Judge James R. Cho.

Prosecutors allege that between July 2024 and December 2025, Brooks repeatedly accepted cash from associates of inmates in exchange for bringing contraband into the facility. On Oct. 18, 2024, according to the release, she allegedly received $5,000 through a payment app from a person who had received the same amount minutes earlier from an inmate's relative. In December 2025, she allegedly exchanged text messages with an inmate who was using a contraband phone.

U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said the alleged conduct endangered staff and inmates for personal gain. Officials with the Justice Department's inspector general and the FBI said they would continue to pursue corruption by prison staff.
If convicted of bribery, Brooks faces up to 15 years in prison, prosecutors said. The charges are allegations, and she is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

greenpoint-luxury-tower-ran-on-generator.title: Greenpoint Luxury Tower Ran on Generator Power for a Month After Fire; Tenants Sue
greenpoint-luxury-tower-ran-on-generator.dek: The Greenpoint, a 463-unit rental tower in Brooklyn, relied on a generator for more than a month after a Sept. 6 electrical fire, and tenants have filed housing court cases.
body: The Greenpoint, a 40-story, 463-unit luxury rental tower at 21 India St. in Brooklyn, ran on generator power for more than a month after an electrical fire knocked it off the grid, Hoodline reported, citing reporting by Gothamist.

The fire broke out around 8 p.m. on Sept. 6, and the FDNY put it out just over an hour later, according to Gothamist. An email reviewed by the outlet indicated that it started in an electrical closet on the eighth floor. Building manager Rose Associates reconnected the electrical system and shut off the generator late on Oct. 7.

Over the past two years, residents filed 272 complaints about hot water and power outages, 191 of them since the fire, and the city's Department of Housing Preservation and Development has issued 38 violations against the building since the fire, Gothamist reported. One resident said the smoke alarms did not go off, and that management did not explain the cause until the following day. Units rent for up to $12,000 a month.

A Rose Associates spokesperson said generator power kept all building services running, attributed the disruptions to an electrical malfunction in a building riser, and said the company followed city rules in restoring power.

Tenants have formed an association, and more than 110 residents signed demands for a full life-safety inspection. On Oct. 7, one tenant filed a case in Brooklyn housing court seeking a building-wide city inspection. Another tenant has separately sued the owner, 19 India Fee Owner LLC, according to the report.

mamdani-orders-nypd-use-of-force-review-.title: Mamdani Orders NYPD Use-of-Force Review After Officer Retires Before Trial
mamdani-orders-nypd-use-of-force-review-.dek: The mayor ordered a review of police use-of-force policies after an officer in a fatal 2024 Queens shooting retired before facing a disciplinary trial.
body: Mayor Zohran Mamdani has ordered a comprehensive review of NYPD use-of-force policies, along with new accountability measures, after an officer involved in the fatal 2024 police shooting of a 19-year-old in Ozone Park, Queens, retired before his disciplinary trial, amNY reported.

City Hall said the review, led by Chief of Department Michael LiPetri and Deputy Commissioner Michael Gerber, is the first of its kind in a decade and will include community input, according to amNY. The administration is adding $2.6 million to the NYPD Office of the Inspector General, which City Hall said would triple its headcount.

The NYPD admitted that it failed to notify the Civilian Complaint Review Board that Officer Salvatore Alongi was seeking retirement, amNY reported. He retired in May with an accidental disability pension, and the CCRB confirmed that he will not face a departmental trial. Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch apologized and called it human error. The department said a civilian employee was demoted and reassigned.

Under the new procedures, retirement applications tied to pending CCRB cases will receive two levels of review, and officers who retire with charges pending will be reported to the state, which can lead to decertification, according to amNY. Police union leaders criticized the review. The young man's parents rejected the human-error explanation and called for Tisch to be fired.

The state attorney general declined to bring criminal charges in December 2025. A CCRB disciplinary trial for the second officer, Matthew Cianfrocco, will go forward. No date has been set, amNY reported.

manhattan-prosecutors-push-to-keep-state.title: Manhattan Prosecutors Push to Keep State Case Against Mangione Alive
manhattan-prosecutors-push-to-keep-state.dek: Prosecutors argued that Luigi Mangione's federal guilty plea should not end the state murder case over the 2024 killing of a health insurance executive.
body: On Friday, Manhattan prosecutors asked a court to let their state murder case against Luigi Mangione go forward despite his guilty plea in federal court, according to an Associated Press report published by NY1.

The state case concerns the December 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson on a Manhattan street. In a court filing, Assistant District Attorney Joel Seidemann and colleagues argued that the state and federal cases involve different harms, different purposes and different crimes, so double jeopardy does not apply, the AP reported.

Mangione's lawyers are seeking dismissal of the state murder and weapons charges, arguing that he is being prosecuted twice for the same event. A ruling is expected in late autumn, according to the AP.

In August, Mangione pleaded guilty to federal stalking and cyberstalking charges and admitted traveling to New York to carry out the killing, the AP reported. In 2024 he had pleaded not guilty to the state murder, weapons and fake-ID charges. If the state case goes to trial, his federal admission could be used against him.

The ruling will decide whether Mangione, 28, faces a state trial in Manhattan, and how much prison time a state conviction could add to what is likely to be a lengthy federal sentence, according to the AP.

judges-hear-9-11-families-case-against-s.title: Judges Hear 9/11 Families' Case Against Saudi Arabia
judges-hear-9-11-families-case-against-s.dek: A federal appeals panel in Manhattan heard arguments on whether U.S. courts have jurisdiction over families' claims that Saudi Arabia aided the Sept. 11 hijackers.
body: On Wednesday, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals in Manhattan heard arguments in the long-running lawsuit brought by families of people killed on Sept. 11, 2001, who argue that the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia helped the attackers, NY1 reported.

The panel is considering only one question: whether federal courts have jurisdiction over Saudi Arabia, which as a nation holds sovereign immunity, according to NY1. A law Congress passed 10 years ago made the suit possible. A year ago, a federal judge denied the kingdom's motion to dismiss.

The families, including members of 9/11 Justice and 9/11 Families United, claim that men who worked for Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Islamic Affairs helped at least two of the hijackers, including by finding them housing in San Diego, and that they knew of the plot, NY1 reported. The families are seeking billions of dollars.

A lawyer for the Saudi government told the panel that the kingdom has never supported al-Qaida and is a U.S. ally. Brett Eagleson, president of 9/11 Justice, who lost his father in the attacks, called the kingdom's position a desperate attempt to avoid accountability, according to NY1. Terry Strada, national chair of 9/11 Families United, urged President Trump to side with the families.

The Saudi consulate did not respond to NY1's request for comment, and lawyers for both sides declined interviews. The appeals court did not say when it will rule. The families hope a trial will begin within the next year.

federal-judge-strikes-down-ice-courthous.title: Federal Judge Strikes Down ICE Courthouse Arrest Policy Nationwide
federal-judge-strikes-down-ice-courthous.dek: Judge P. Kevin Castel ruled that the policy behind mass arrests at immigration courts, including at 26 Federal Plaza, was arbitrary and capricious.
body: On Oct. 1, U.S. District Judge P. Kevin Castel struck down an ICE policy that led to mass detentions inside immigration courthouses, among them hundreds at 26 Federal Plaza in Lower Manhattan, amNY reported. The ruling applies nationwide and took effect immediately.

Castel found the legal basis for the detentions arbitrary and capricious, according to amNY. ICE must now return to a 2021 policy that allows arrests at or near immigration courts only in limited circumstances.

The lawsuit was filed on Aug. 1, 2025, by a coalition that included the New York Civil Liberties Union, the ACLU and Make the Road New York, amNY reported. In a March filing, then-U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton and the NYCLU said ICE had misrepresented its authority to make arrests inside immigration courts. The final ruling affirms an earlier stay and extends it across the country.

Amy Belsher of the NYCLU called the decision a major win for noncitizens attending their hearings, and Harold Solis of Make the Road New York said it ends the practice of arresting immigrants for showing up to court, according to amNY.

Courthouse sources told amNY that arrests have slowed but still occur, with one reported the week before the ruling, and that fear of detention led some people to skip their hearings. Under federal law, people who miss hearings can be ordered removed in absentia. amNY did not report an appeal.

federal-monitor-finds-nearly-10000-nypd-.title: Federal Monitor Finds Nearly 10,000 NYPD Street Stops Missing From Records
federal-monitor-finds-nearly-10000-nypd-.dek: The court-appointed stop-and-frisk monitor estimated that about one in four NYPD investigative stops in 2025 went undocumented.
body: The court-appointed monitor overseeing NYPD stop-and-frisk reforms has reported that officers failed to properly document nearly 10,000 investigative stops in 2025, amNY reported.

According to the report by monitor Mylan L. Denerstein, 9,641 so-called Terry stops went undocumented and 25,936 were documented, meaning roughly one in four was never recorded, amNY reported. A Terry stop, based on reasonable suspicion, allows officers to briefly detain someone, and it requires a formal stop report.

The monitor's team reviewed body camera footage and found that officers had recorded some of these stops as lower-level encounters, which do not require paperwork, according to amNY. Underreporting fell to 18.4% in the fourth quarter of 2025, against an estimated 27.1% for the full year.

The NYPD acknowledged that more work is needed but said the trend is improving, noting that reported stops fell from more than 680,000 in 2011 to fewer than 30,000 in 2025, amNY reported. Legal Aid Society attorney Karina Tefft called the findings a fundamental failure of accountability, and attorney Jonathan Moore urged the court to take aggressive action.
The report has been released. amNY did not report any court ruling or remedy in response to it.

three-men-sentenced-for-harlem-gang-kill.title: Three Men Sentenced to 22 Years to Life in 2025 Harlem Killing
three-men-sentenced-for-harlem-gang-kill.dek: Three men convicted in the fatal May 2025 attack on a 33-year-old man outside a Harlem deli were each sentenced to 22 years to life in prison, amNY reported.
body: Three men convicted in the killing of a 33-year-old man outside a Harlem deli were each sentenced on Tuesday, Sept. 29, to 22 years to life in prison, according to amNY.
Naquan Anderson, Trevor Carpenter and Alvin Nelson were convicted in Manhattan court on Aug. 11 of gang assault, along with murder and manslaughter, the outlet reported.

According to police, the attack took place at about 5:14 a.m. on May 3, 2025, outside a deli on Frederick Douglass Boulevard near West 141st Street. Police said it followed an argument between the victim and Nelson, after which the three men chased him. Police said Nelson and Anderson stabbed the man while Carpenter beat him. The three then left in Carpenter's vehicle. The man was pronounced dead at Harlem Hospital, the report said.
Nelson was arrested on May 16, 2025, Carpenter on May 22 and Anderson on June 9, according to amNY.

Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg said the defendants turned a personal dispute into deadly violence against an unarmed man, and expressed hope that the sentences would bring a measure of justice to his family, the outlet reported. The victim's sister told the New York Daily News that he had recently returned home and had no conflicts with anyone.

five-new-restaurant-openings-and-dining-.title: New Openings Include Cambridge Robata Bar, Second Michette Bakery
five-new-restaurant-openings-and-dining-.dek: Boston.com's weekly dining roundup lists openings in Cambridge, Braintree and downtown, along with a poutine festival in the Seaport.
body: The latest dining openings in the Boston area include a Japanese charcoal-grill bar, a second location of a French bakery and an expanding ramen chain, according to Boston.com's weekly roundup by Nathan Tavares.

EnYa Robatayaki & Sake Bar is coming to 125 River St. in Cambridge, the former What A Soup space. It will serve skewers grilled over charcoal, and sake, in an izakaya-style setting, Boston.com reported. The opening is expected this fall, with details to follow on Instagram.
Michette Bakery has opened a second location, at 305 Webster Ave. in Inman Square. It serves croissants, pastries, breads and savory items, along with coffee and drinks, according to the roundup.

Ramen Haven, a local chain that started in Berlin, Massachusetts, opens at the South Shore Mall in Braintree in October and at 832 Commonwealth Ave. in December, Boston.com reported. The Sports Bra, a bar that shows only women's sports, plans to open at 2 Broad St. downtown by the end of the year.
The roundup also listed PoutineFest at Harpoon, 306 Northern Ave. in the Seaport, on Saturday, Oct. 17, from 11:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Tickets start at $54.99.

new-restaurant-with-skyline-views-opens-.title: The Moseley Opens on Ninth Floor of South Station Tower
new-restaurant-with-skyline-views-opens-.dek: A 10,000-square-foot restaurant from Chicago-based Episcope Hospitality opened Oct. 5 above South Station, looking out on the city skyline, Boston.com reported.
body: The Moseley opened to the public on Oct. 5 on the ninth floor of South Station Tower, 680 Atlantic Ave., Boston.com reported. The space runs roughly 10,000 square feet and looks out over the downtown skyline.

The operator is Chicago-based Episcope Hospitality. Its CEO and co-founder, David Morton, is the son of Arnold Morton, co-founder of Morton's The Steakhouse, according to the report. Morton described the style to Boston.com as casual fine dining built around quality ingredients and simple preparation. Episcope also runs two other concepts in the tower, open only to tenants and residents.

Hours are 11:30 a.m. to 9 p.m. Monday through Friday for lunch and dinner, and 5 p.m. to 9 p.m. Saturday for dinner. The restaurant also hosts private events, the report said. The menu includes a crab cake, tuna tartare, a lobster roll, a dry-aged sirloin burger, a 10-ounce filet mignon and miso black cod, according to Boston.com. The report did not list prices.

Boston firm Perkins&Will designed the room, with curved white oak ceilings, wood paneling and bronze accents meant to recall rail cars of the late 1800s, according to the report. The name comes from Alex Moseley, who ran a leather business on nearby South Street in that era and helped shape what became the Leather District.
South Station Tower, a 51-story mixed-use building, was completed in 2025, Boston.com reported.

five-new-restaurant-openings-and-dining-.title: Smashburgers, Uyghur Noodles and a Spice Festival in Boston Dining News
five-new-restaurant-openings-and-dining-.dek: Boston.com's Oct. 2 roundup covers new locations for 7th Street Burger, a Watertown Uyghur takeout spot, a downtown cafe and a West Roxbury burger restaurant.
body: Several restaurants are opening or expanding around Greater Boston this fall, according to a dining roundup published Oct. 2 by Boston.com.

7th Street Burger, a New York-based smashburger chain with existing locations on Newbury Street and in South Boston, plans a 46-seat restaurant at 880 Broadway in Saugus in October and a 22-seat location at 37 Brattle St. in Harvard Square in early 2027, the report said.

In Watertown, Adila Sadir, who runs Silk Road Uyghur Cuisine in Cambridge, is preparing to open Badam Uyghur Cuisine at 58 Mt. Auburn St. in November, according to Boston.com. The spot will have roughly 16 seats and focus on takeout: hand-pulled noodles, lamb kebabs and rice pilaf.

Downtown, MOTW Coffee & Pastries was scheduled to open in mid-October at 45 Broad St., Boston.com reported. The cafe is the retail arm of Muslims of the World, a nonprofit that provides humanitarian aid. It plans to serve chai, lattes, matcha and tiramisu.

In West Roxbury, Yeanie's Burgers and Social opened in September at 1761 Centre St., after delays, according to the report. It is the seventh restaurant for Phi Pham and his wife, Yeanie Bach, and it shares a menu of smash burgers, fried chicken sandwiches and shakes with the Dorchester location.
The roundup also listed Spicetober Fest, a free festival of spicy food, chef demonstrations and live music, held Saturday, Oct. 3, at City Hall Plaza.

boston-magazine-october-guide-to-new-pla.title: Boston Magazine's October Guide Highlights New Restaurants and Bars
boston-magazine-october-guide-to-new-pla.dek: The magazine's monthly list includes a Montreal-inspired spot in Fort Point, a soju distillery in Mission Hill and a rum lounge coming to South Boston.
body: Boston Magazine's October guide to new places to eat and drink around Greater Boston lists more than 20 new or changing restaurants, cafes and bars, according to the list by food editor Rachel Leah Blumenthal.

Among the new restaurants, the magazine highlighted Celine, at 324 A St. in Fort Point, a Montreal-inspired French-Canadian spot from the team behind SRV, Gufo and Salty Pig. It also named Zhu, at 903 Boylston St. in Back Bay, a multi-level Chinese seafood and dim sum restaurant in soft opening. In Groton, chef Will Gilson of Cambridge's Puritan & Company is behind Puritan Tavern, a more casual New England tavern at 20 Station Ave., the guide said.

On the drinks side, the guide lists Namu Distilling Co., at 89 Heath St. in Mission Hill, which the magazine described as New England's first soju distillery, and Overproof Cocktail Lounge, a rum-focused bar at 85 Damrell St. in South Boston expected to open later in October. The list also includes Bloom in the Seaport; C'Yool, a Yemeni cafe and bakery in the South End; and Pomona Cafe & Wine Bar in East Boston.

The guide also noted established names trying something new. Brookline Lunch has expanded to 108 L St. in South Boston. Quincy's Rubato, led by Top Chef finalist Laurence Louie, was set to begin regular dinner service on Oct. 9. And the Lao pop-up Phaeng & Phiu has taken up residence at Shore Leave in the South End for its final months, according to Boston Magazine.
Shore Leave and its sibling bars are scheduled to close at the end of the year, the magazine reported.

five-boston-restaurants-to-watch-in-octo.title: Five Boston Restaurants to Watch in October
five-boston-restaurants-to-watch-in-octo.dek: Boston.com's October picks include a Yemeni coffeehouse in the South End, a Roxbury jazz cafe, a Mission Hill soju distillery, a Back Bay sushi pop-up and a three-level Chinese restaurant.
body: Boston.com has named five new or recently opened restaurants it is eager to try in October, in a list by Jillian Dara published Oct. 1.

C'Yool, a new Yemeni coffeehouse and bakery at 600 Harrison Ave. in the South End, roasts its beans on site and serves breads such as sabaya along with traditional coffee drinks, according to the list. In Roxbury, Jazz Urbane Cafe, at 2300 Washington St., has opened as a live music and arts venue. Its restaurant menu includes brunch dishes and shrimp and grits, and film screenings and theater are planned, Boston.com reported.

NAMU Distilling Company, at 89 Heath St. in Mission Hill, is a Korean-American craft distillery founded by Will Blessing and Josh Moss.
